body:
Tested locally, it works as expected in all rendering methods[^1].

**Testing project:** [test_lightmapgi_vram_compress.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18115306/test_lightmapgi_vram_compress.zip)

<details open>

<summary>PC specifications</summary>

- **CPU:** Intel Core i9-13900K
- **GPU:** NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090
- **RAM:** 64 GB (2×32 GB DDR5-5800 C30)
- **SSD:** Solidigm P44 Pro 2 TB
- **OS:** Linux (Fedora 41)
</details>

On the above PC, import speeds are roughly the same between VRAM Uncompressed and VRAM Compressed on my system, although I tested this on a debug build (VRAM Uncompressed will surely be faster on an optimized build).

This reduces lightmap memory utilization by a factor of 4 or 6 (depending on the algorithm used), which is pretty significant on large scenes. On the test project, it decreases from 96 MB down to 16 MB using `BPTC_RGBFU`. In terms of quality, it's undistinguishable from VRAM Compressed outside of side-by-side comparisons (and even then, differences are difficult to spot). This is far cry from previous attempts at using S3TC on compressed lightmaps :slightly_smiling_face: 

The same applies to shadowmasks, although they already seemed to use VRAM compression before this change.

However, VRAM compression is only set if you remove the existing EXR file and bake lightmaps again. Baking lightmaps without removing the existing EXR file first will keep the compression mode to the previous VRAM Uncompressed.

Also, another issue I noticed is that when in Compatibility, attempting to reimport the shadowmask texture with the VRAM Compressed import mode will make it look blocky until the scene is reloaded:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/60a91843-3f24-4b07-9b07-92148122768c)

This is also printed on reimport:

```
ERROR: Cannot convert to (or from) compressed formats. Use compress() and decompress() instead.
```

[^1]: Betsy requires support for RenderingDevice-based rendering methods, but it can be used while in Compatibility, just like LightmapGI baking.
Woohoo! This is fantastic news for Lightmap users.
